The minarets, domes and houses are Ottoman or later; the Sea Castle, its bridge and the line of the harbour are what the view keeps of the medieval town, and even the castle was repaired by the Mamluks after 1291 and restored in the seventeenth century.

summary: Sidon on the Lebanese coast: a Fatimid garrison port taken by Baldwin I of Jerusalem and Sigurd of Norway in 1110, seat of the crusader lordship of the Grenier family, fortified with its Sea Castle in 1227–1228, and lost by the Templars to the Mamluks in July 1291.
overview: Sidon was a small Byzantine and early Islamic port that became one of the great baronies of the crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem. The Grenier family held it for 150 years, losing it to Saladin in 1187 and recovering it in 1197; Louis IX rebuilt its walls in 1253, the Mongols sacked it in 1260, and the Templars who bought it gave up its Sea Castle to the Mamluks in 1291.
knownFor: Seat of the crusader lordship of Sidon, one of the four great baronies of the Kingdom of Jerusalem
Taken in 1110 by Baldwin I of Jerusalem with the fleet of Sigurd of Norway
The Sea Castle on its offshore island, begun in 1227–1228
The land castle of St Louis, on the ancient tell south of the town
Sacked by the Mongols in 1260 and held by the Templars until 1291

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Sidon stands on a low promontory on the southern Lebanese coast, about 40 kilometres from both Beirut and Tyre, with a rocky island sheltering its northern harbour. The crusaders called it Sagette, Arabic writers Sayda. A Fatimid garrison port, it became in 1110 the seat of one of the four great baronies of the Kingdom of Jerusalem.
That crusader period left the two castles that still frame the old town, one on the island and one on the ancient tell, before the last Templar garrison gave Sidon up to the Mamluks in July 1291.

contentSections.title: Phoenician and Byzantine Sidon
paragraphs: A leading Phoenician city, famous for glass and purple dye, Sidon became a Roman colony and then a Byzantine bishopric under the metropolitan of Tyre. After the earthquake of 551 wrecked Berytus, the modern Beirut, its law school took refuge in Sidon, but the town was small when the Arabs came.

contentSections.title: Arab and Fatimid rule, 636–1107
paragraphs: Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan and his brother Mu'awiya took Sidon, Beirut and Byblos after the fall of Damascus, in 636 or 637 (the Arabic histories, written two centuries later, differ). Under the Umayyads and Abbasids it was a small fortified port of the province of Damascus.

The Fatimid caliphs of Cairo, who fought the Seljuk rulers of Damascus for the coast, recovered Sidon for the last time in 1088 and strengthened it in 1098. The Persian traveller Nasir-i Khusraw, passing through in 1047, found a stone wall with three gates, a Friday mosque laid with patterned mats, and a market so richly decorated that he thought the town was expecting the sultan, until he was told it always looked like that.

contentSections.title: The crusader conquest, 1108–1110
paragraphs: In 1108, the usual dating, Baldwin I of Jerusalem attacked Sidon with ships from Italian cities, but an Egyptian fleet beat the Italians outside the harbour, Turkish horsemen rode from Damascus to relieve the town, and he withdrew.

In 1110 King Sigurd of Norway reached Acre with, by the saga's count, sixty ships. From about 19 October Baldwin's army invested Sidon by land while the Norwegians closed the sea and a Venetian fleet kept off the Fatimid squadron at Tyre. The siege of Sidon lasted 47 days, and the town surrendered on terms between 3 and 5 December 1110, the sources differing by two days. By Arabic accounts the governor, garrison and many townspeople left for Damascus, and those who stayed were soon made to pay 20,000 dinars.

contentSections.title: The Grenier lordship, 1110–1187
paragraphs: Baldwin gave Sidon to Eustace Grenier, a Flemish knight who already held Caesarea. With Beaufort, the inland castle King Fulk took in 1139 and granted to its lords, it ranked among the kingdom's four great baronies. Eustace was regent during the captivity of Baldwin II of Jerusalem in 1123 and died that June.

Eustace's grandson Reginald, lord by 1171, spoke Arabic, married Agnes of Courtenay, mother of Baldwin IV, and in 1174 backed Raymond III of Tripoli for the regency. He escaped from Hattin with the rearguard in July 1187, and Saladin entered Sidon without a fight later that summer and pulled down its defences.

contentSections.title: Saladin and the Frankish return, 1187–1227
paragraphs: Reginald held out at Beaufort. In 1189 he offered Saladin the castle, and even his own conversion to Islam, and used the months of grace to repair and stock it; when the ruse was exposed he was imprisoned, and the garrison surrendered on 22 April 1190 in exchange for his release.

The crusade sent by the emperor Henry VI occupied the ruined town in the autumn of 1197. King Aimery of Lusignan restored it to Reginald under a truce of 1198 with al-Adil which, by the Arabic accounts, divided Sidon between the Franks and the Ayyubids.

contentSections.title: The Sea Castle and Louis IX, 1227–1254
paragraphs: In 1227 crusaders who went east ahead of the emperor Frederick II expelled the Damascene troops still in Sidon and fortified the island off the harbour, building the Sea Castle. Reginald's son Balian, lord from 1202, became Frederick's chief ally among the barons, his envoy to al-Kamil and, from 1231, co-regent.

Troops from Damascus overran Sidon in July 1249, while Louis IX's army was in Egypt, and again in 1253 as his workmen were rebuilding the walls. Jean de Joinville says the commander withdrew into the castle in the sea while the townspeople were cut down. Louis helped carry the decaying bodies to burial with his own hands and rebuilt the walls and the land castle, which still bears his name, before sailing home in 1254.

contentSections.title: Mongols, Templars and Mamluks, 1260–1291
paragraphs: In 1260, while the Mongol general Kitbuqa held Damascus, Balian's son Julian raided the Beqaa valley and killed Kitbuqa's nephew in an ambush. The Mongols sacked Sidon in revenge, though the Sea Castle held, and the ruined Julian sold Sidon and Beaufort to the Knights Templar in 1260 or 1261.

Baybars took Beaufort in 1268. After Acre fell on 18 May 1291 the surviving Templars brought their treasury to Sidon and elected Thibaud Gaudin grand master there. Too few to hold the walls, they withdrew to the Sea Castle; when the emir Sanjar al-Shuja'i began a causeway to the island they sailed for Tortosa, and on 14 July the Mamluks entered the castle and ordered it destroyed.

contentSections.title: Mamluk Sidon
paragraphs: The Mamluks demolished the fortifications of the conquered coast so that no crusade could land and hold them, and at Sidon, by later local tradition, wrecked the harbour. The Sea Castle was partly pulled down and then repaired, with a small mosque attributed to the sultan al-Ashraf Khalil.

The town stayed exposed to the sea: raiders from Europe landed in 1306 and carried off sixty townspeople, whom the deputy governor of Safad ransomed for 30,000 dirhams. Abu al-Fida described Sidon in 1321 as a small town of the province of Damascus with a citadel, and the pilgrim Ludolf of Sudheim found high towers and walls around a deserted town. The Ottomans took it in 1516.

contentSections.title: Rulers and notable figures
paragraphs: The Grenier lords held Sidon for 150 years: Eustace (1110–1123), Gerard (1123 to the 1160s), Reginald (about 1171–1187 and 1198–1202), Balian (1202 to about 1240) and Julian (about 1240–1260), whose sons kept only the title; the last died in 1289. The Templars governed from 1260 until 1291.

Reginald is the best recorded. William of Tyre blamed him for abandoning the fugitives from Jacob's Ford in 1179, Arabic writers described his ruse at Beaufort, and a thirteenth-century genealogy of the crusader nobility called him extremely ugly and very wise.

contentSections.title: The medieval town
paragraphs: Medieval Sidon filled the promontory between two bays, walled on the landward side, with its anchorage in the northern harbour and a castle at each end. The Sea Castle, joined to the shore by a bridge about 80 metres long, is two towers linked by a wall, with Roman columns laid crosswise through the masonry as bonding; the lower part of the eastern tower is crusader work beneath a Mamluk storey. The land castle on the tell at the south-eastern edge of the old town is a thirteenth-century ruin, called the castle of St Louis in French and Qalaat al-Muizz in Arabic, after the Fatimid caliph al-Mu'izz, to whom tradition credits its first fortress. Near the northern shore the Great Omari Mosque occupies a fortified hall with a large church, said to have been built by the Hospitallers in about 1261 and made a mosque after 1291.

contentSections.title: Sidon beyond its walls
paragraphs: The capture of 1110 gave the Kingdom of Jerusalem the coast between Beirut and Tyre and left Tyre, which held out until 1124, isolated. In Norway the siege became the climax of Sigurd's expedition in skaldic verse and in Snorri Sturluson's Heimskringla, and the splinter of the True Cross that Baldwin gave Sigurd was granted on condition that it go to the shrine of Saint Olaf. Reginald's Arabic made him a go-between for Saladin and the leaders of the Third Crusade, and in 1291 the Sea Castle was one of the Templars' last footholds on the mainland.

timeline.title: Mongol sack
timeline.description: Kitbuqa's troops sack the town; Julian sells the lordship to the Knights Templar that year or the next.

timeline.title: Ottoman conquest
timeline.description: Sidon passes to the Ottomans with the rest of Syria.
